barCharacter: Vera Oberlin. Same comic job as Vesper: the one at the top of the hierarchy whose approval everyone is chasing, who rates losers and never asks permission. Vera's 12: #12 career/losers, #45 chore being this beautiful, #47 cover up the literal murder, #48 Right. Now., #52 four drinks ending in poison, #51 feminism talk as an order, #49 SUCH a good advisor, #50 most trusted advisor, #46 Cools over Un-Cools, #56 50 Monster Dollars, #53 not a death stare this time, #54 hair and a cattle prod. Our 12: the five bestLines plus 'You read that like your own obituary, approvingly.', 'Prince, I don't believe a word of it, and I'm keeping the stationery.', 'That's the show. Go to sleep. I won't.', 'Brock, the last thing proud of me rusted, so tell me why you are.', 'One truth, one lie, and I'll know, because liars breathe in before the true bit.', 'Sorry, Tilly. See? It's easy. Goodnight.', 'Brock, you'd be wonderful at seven a.m., and I don't exist then.' Voice: with names covered, Vera is known by shape (the repeat-then-turn, the two-word imperative, the 'Right?' tag that assumes you're complicit). Ours is known mostly by topic, the radio nouns. Take the nouns out of 'You read that like your own obituary, approvingly', 'Sorry, Tilly. See? It's easy. Goodnight.' and the stationery line and they are Maximilian lines. Construction: about level. Ours is tight, with real turns, and our top 12 has fewer filler lines than Vera's (her #46, #49 and #50 are plain prompts). Quotable: Vera's career line and the poison line are the clips people repeat. Ours has two of that strength (the Brock hours line and the page turn), so in doubt the bar wins.

templates: MASTER SHAPE: '[Name], [clause], and [tail]'. 122 of 276 lines contain ', and '. It is how she is recognised, more than any attitude, and it makes the whole bank one rhythm.
'[Name], [scene-setter], so [order]': 11 of the 16 oneOnOne prompts, plus about 12 questions and twistIntros (23 lines with ', so ').

holdCard is four stamped frames used 3 to 4 times each: 'I came in wanting X, and look who's left' (4), 'The one I'm keeping X, and so did the other' (4), 'What I wanted was X, and you both Y' (4), 'Stand still, both of you, ...' (3), plus 'Both of you X. One of you Y.' (3) and 'You both X, and ...' (3).
cardHint: 'it came down to X, and Y' (4), 'I'm cutting {name} over/on/for' (4), 'Goodnight, {name}, and ...' (3), 'I kept hearing/waiting' (4), '{name}, who/where ...?' (4).
react simile to a radio noun: 'that had the [quality] of a [noun]' / 'like a [noun]' / 'as [x] as a [noun]' (about 9).
charmed reactions as handing over a bulletin: 'you can read the [closures/results/weather]' (5).
keepsake when charmed: 'I'm writing that on / putting that on / going on my [object]' (7, including the pickFrame 'wrote it on the back of my hand').
cut as 'you [sounded/talked] like [simile], all night' (5 of 16 cuts).
pick as '[Name], you're picked, and ...' / 'it's you, and' / 'I'm keeping you, and' (6 of 16).
tail explainer ', which is [how/the only/more than] ...' (10).
ruleBreaks: Word limits: none over (checked every line against its category cap, with slots counted as one word and {hook} as up to five).
No em dashes, no emoji, no exclamation marks, no lists, no therapy talk, no 'as an AI', nothing beyond PG-13, no real person or brand.

Breaks the persona's 'never three short sentences in a row': 'Don't talk with your mouth full. It carries. Sixty miles.' / 'Caller, that's very old. So am I. Mine aged better.' / 'Sorry, Tilly. See? It's easy. Goodnight.' / 'That's the show. Go to sleep. I won't.' / 'Brock. You're too loud for my hours. I'm changing my hours.' / '{card}. I left it out like a porch light. Nobody came.' Several of these are among her best lines, so the rule, not the lines, is what should change.

Breaks the persona's 'never joke from the suitor's job or costume': 'Brock, every dog in range has started barking.' / 'Tilly, hands behind your back is how they rob stations.' / 'Crumb, don't be kind, how done do I look?' / 'Prince, I'm writing back, and I've enclosed a small processing fee.'
Stock romance filler, borderline: '{card}. {name} found it without a map, the way I like being found.'

Too nice for a star (warmth with no sting): 'Crumb, you can have the last biscuit in the tin.' / 'Brock, I turned you down, and you stayed sweet.' / 'Vex, that goes in the shoebox with the good letters.' / 'Stand still, both of you, you each said something frightened, and it worked.' / 'You both apologised on my air, and I've decided that's what I like.'
Too nice for a cut (ends on a consolation): 'Crumb, you're going back to the kitchen, where the radio's always on.' / 'Tilly, you were very kind tonight, and I can't broadcast kind.'

Register slip: 'Plan our date for five dollars, no wifi, and it has to reach my chair.' (dollars in an otherwise British small-hours world of bins, biscuits, licence people and the shipping-forecast).
biggestGap: Vesper is recognised by her vocabulary (radio nouns), not by sentence shape: 122 of 276 lines are '[Name], [clause], and [radio-noun tail]'. Next pass, keep ', and' to at most one line in five. Make her default shape the status flip her best lines already use: one plain statement of her total control over the air or the hours, with the suitor shrinking against it ('I muted the moon landing. I can mute you.', 'I'm changing my hours.', 'and I write those'). Lift the persona's ban on short drops, because those lines are the ones that work.
